For him, the movement toward truth, or knowledge, begins with reason itself, with what he saw as the natural light of the mind.
Knowledge therefore begins with intuition: the mind’s direct recognition of self-evident truths already present in the human soul.
Descartes regarded the soul as a substance existing in its own right, independent of the body. The body, in turn, was another substance existing in its own right.
Given this philosophical basis for Descartes’s method of doubt, we have to ask: did Taha Hussein adopt the method together with all these philosophical foundations?
Did he truly adopt it as a philosophical method?
Or did he understand it in a simpler way, seeing only its formal side while missing its deeper philosophical content?
In other words, did he take only the immediate, everyday meaning of the word “doubt,” separately from its Cartesian implications for the theory of knowledge?
To answer this question, we need to look at two sides of the issue.
The first is the scientific position toward Cartesian doubt itself.
The second is Taha Hussein’s own practical use of it.
On the first point, scientific analysis rejects the philosophical propositions on which Descartes’s method of doubt is based. It does so for the following reasons:
1 — At its foundation, the method rests on Descartes’s famous proposition: “I think, therefore I am.”

This proposition places Descartes directly in the idealist camp, because it establishes existence through thought. In other words, it denies the objective character of existence: the fact that existence is independent of consciousness, or thought, and comes before it.
2 — The method asks human consciousness to do something that it simply cannot do: eliminate the role of sensory knowledge from the process through which we arrive at truth.

The role of sensory experience is an objective fact. It cannot be abolished by an act of personal will, even when that act of will takes the form of a philosophical proposition or is supported by one.
3 — The method would require us to discard all the knowledge that human consciousness has gained over its enormously long history.

This accumulated knowledge has become part of the historical formation of human consciousness itself. It has become an objective historical reality. It cannot simply be removed from consciousness, even by an act of consciousness itself.
4 — After “cleansing” human consciousness of everything it has learned through history, the method would return it to zero.
It would return consciousness to a childhood that humanity left behind thousands of years ago.

If such a thing were even possible, human consciousness would then have to spend thousands of new years passing once again through all the stages needed to reach the level it had already reached by the time of Descartes.
This completely “unhistorical” process is objectively impossible.
Rejecting these Cartesian propositions does not mean that everything human consciousness has learned throughout history is absolutely true.
Whether this inherited body of knowledge is correct or mistaken, wholly or partly, is a separate question that has to be studied on a different level.
Still, it is useful here to summarize the scientific position.

Historical materialist analysis sees the knowledge accumulated by human consciousness during its long development as a series of historical forms of consciousness. Each belongs to a particular stage in that development.
These forms of consciousness are direct or indirect reflections of the corresponding stages through which social reality itself has developed.
That does not mean, first, that these reflections must perfectly match the social reality that produced them.
Nor does it mean, second, that they must perfectly match the objective and absolute truths of the universe.
There can be many differences between the world as human consciousness understands it and the objective reality of nature and society.

But as human consciousness has developed—together with human societies and the natural sciences—each historical stage has revealed new relative truths and, in doing so, exposed errors in earlier forms of knowledge.
When we study that earlier knowledge and try to distinguish what was right from what was wrong, we therefore need a scientific method.
That method does not begin by “doubting” earlier knowledge in the Cartesian sense of removing it from consciousness or “cleansing” the mind of it.
It begins, first, by treating that knowledge as an objective reality with a history of its own—something with a real historical existence that cannot simply be erased.
Second, it studies that knowledge as something whose development was objectively connected with the development of the material and social reality from which it arose and through which it changed.
Now we come to the second side of the issue: Taha Hussein’s practical use of Cartesian “doubt” in his study of pre-Islamic literature.
Here it seems clear to us that he takes the idea of “doubt” only in its formal sense, without adopting the philosophical theory of knowledge on which Descartes built it.
It is true that Taha Hussein refers to the philosophical form of the method when he says:
“In literature, I want to adopt the philosophical method introduced by Descartes for investigating the truths of things at the beginning of the modern age.”

“The basic rule of this method is that the researcher must free himself from everything he knew before and begin his investigation with a mind completely empty of everything previously said about the subject.”
It is also true that, when defining how he intends to apply the method, he writes:

“When we begin to study Arabic literature and its history, we must forget our national feelings in all their particular forms. We must forget our religious feelings and everything connected with them. We must also forget whatever clashes with those national and religious feelings.
“We must bind ourselves to nothing and submit to nothing except the methods of sound scientific research.”
But what, exactly, does all this mean?
From its tone, context, and indeed from the words themselves, we can understand it only in one way.
Taha Hussein wants to study Arabic literature and its history after freeing himself from the traditionalist view of this heritage: the view that simply accepts it as true.

He wants to free himself from automatically accepting the opinions, positions, and reports handed down by transmitters, chroniclers, storytellers, hadith scholars, Qurʾānic commentators, and the writers who recorded Arab-Islamic history.

This kind of freedom in studying the heritage is what Taha Hussein means when he says that “the researcher must free himself from everything he knew before and begin his investigation with a mind empty of everything previously said about the subject.”

It is also what he means when he says that “we must forget our national feelings in all their particular forms,” “forget our religious feelings and everything connected with them,” and “forget whatever clashes with those national and religious feelings.”
He is calling for freedom from inherited social influences and inherited restraints on the way we understand the heritage today.

Taha Hussein therefore wants to approach Arabic literature and its history by doubting these inherited influences and restraints, so that “we bind ourselves to nothing and submit to nothing except the methods of sound scientific research.”
Put differently, he wants us to study the heritage without prejudice either for it or against it.
He wants us to free ourselves from both traditional ways of approaching it.
Nothing Taha Hussein says about his method in On Pre-Islamic Literature points to anything substantially different from this.

Taha Hussein is very far from wanting to erase the Arabic literature and history preserved in our consciousness. He is not calling for the destruction of the sources that make up the actual historical body of this heritage. Nor is he asking us to “cleanse” our consciousness of these sources accumulated through history or to erase this objective historical reality from Arab consciousness altogether.
What he wants is something much more specific.
He wants to produce a new, contemporary understanding of this historical reality, free from the traditionalist understanding of it and subject only to “the methods of sound scientific research.”

Yet although Taha Hussein’s use of “doubt” in studying pre-Islamic literature has only a formal connection with the philosophical foundations of Cartesian doubt, we must still recognize the enormous positive role he played as a pioneer in the study of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.
His attempt to create a new, modern way of understanding this heritage was itself important.
So was his attempt to bring the modern “methods of scientific research” into that work.
In the 1920s, these two things together amounted to an intellectual breakthrough of great historical importance.
But once we move beyond this pioneering achievement, other aspects of Taha Hussein’s work appear as weaknesses in his method.

For one thing, he became so absorbed by doubt about the authenticity of pre-Islamic poetry that “doubt” almost became the reason for the investigation, rather than one possible conclusion produced by it.
For another, he often carried this method of doubt beyond what “sound scientific research” itself requires: a historical understanding of the reality being studied.
His commitment to doubting the attribution of pre-Islamic poetry became so strong that he stripped almost all this poetry of its historical value for the period before Islam.

Even the “very small amount” of literature that he accepted as genuinely pre-Islamic came to represent nothing and prove nothing. He said that it should not be relied upon to reconstruct a true literary picture of the pre-Islamic period.

He then made the categorical judgment that our knowledge of the pre-Islamic period should rest not on the poetry attributed to it, but “on the Qurʾān on the one hand, and history and legend on the other.”
He also argued that this poetry should not be used as evidence in interpreting the Qurʾān and hadith. Instead, the Qurʾān and hadith should be used to explain and interpret the poetry.
“Sound scientific research” rejects absolute judgments of this kind.
In principle, it rejects any absolute conclusion that is not supported by definite evidence from reality.
Yet On Pre-Islamic Literature was unable to provide evidence strong enough to justify conclusions this absolute.
We agree with Taha Hussein that much of the poetry attributed to the pre-Islamic period is of doubtful authenticity and that some of it was undoubtedly fabricated.
We also agree with most of the reasons he gives for doubting particular poems or judging them to be later inventions.
But we still cannot agree that poetry of doubtful authenticity, or even poetry known to have been fabricated, has no historical value for the pre-Islamic period immediately before the rise of Islam.
Indeed, we can say that the historical value of this later fabricated poetry does not differ in any fundamental way from the historical value of genuinely pre-Islamic poetry itself.
There are two reasons for this, and no scientific method can ignore them when studying literary phenomena of this kind.

The first is that the gap between genuinely pre-Islamic poetry and poetry fabricated shortly after the rise of Islam was not large enough to create a major difference in their historical relationship to Arab society.
Both kinds of poetry were connected with historical features shared by these two closely overlapping periods.
This applies both to the development of Arab society and to the development of Arabic poetry itself.

We can even appeal to Taha Hussein himself here. Whether he was right or wrong, he wrote that he knew of no nation that had held so firmly to literary conservatism, introducing change only gradually, as the Arabs had done.
“The life of the pre-Islamic Arabs,” he says, “is visible in the poetry of al-Farazdaq, Jarīr, Dhū al-Rumma, al-Akhṭal, al-Rāʿī, and others.”
The second point follows from the very conditions under which Islamic-period poets and transmitters fabricated poetry and attributed it to the pre-Islamic period.
By definition, this fabricated poetry had to resemble genuine pre-Islamic poetry in both form and content. It had to fit the historical features of pre-Islamic Arab society.
Otherwise, the whole act of fabrication would have been pointless.
